title: Management of Inventory
outcomes: Explain the objectives and costs of inventory.
Compute EOQ, evaluate discounts and set stock levels.
Apply ABC, VED, FSN and JIT ideas.

meta.exam_tip: For discount questions, put EOQ and each discount quantity side by side with all three costs.

concepts.title: Objectives of inventory management
body: Inventory (raw materials, WIP, finished goods, stores) is often the largest current asset. Management aims to keep enough to avoid stock-outs and production stoppages while minimising holding and ordering costs and the risk of obsolescence.
Costs: ordering costs (placing orders, receiving, inspection), carrying costs (storage, insurance, interest on funds, obsolescence), and stock-out costs (lost sales, idle time).
Inventory policy affects working capital, liquidity and profitability; it is linked to production planning and purchasing.
concepts.analogy: The right stock is enough to keep the wheels turning — and no more.
concepts.work: Overstocking fashion goods risks markdowns; understocking spare parts risks downtime.

concepts.title: EOQ, quantity discounts and stock levels
body: EOQ = √(2AO ÷ C): A stands for yearly demand, O for the cost of placing one order, and C for the yearly cost of holding one unit. At EOQ, ordering cost equals carrying cost and their total is minimum.
Quantity discounts: compare total cost (purchase + ordering + carrying) at EOQ with that at each discount quantity; accept the lowest.

Stock levels: re-order level = maximum usage × maximum lead time; minimum = ROL − normal usage × normal lead time; maximum = ROL + ROQ − minimum usage × minimum lead time; danger level = normal usage × lead time for emergency purchase; average stock = (min + max) ÷ 2 or min + ½ ROQ. Safety stock buffers uncertainty in usage and lead time.
concepts.analogy: EOQ balances two costs; stock levels translate it into signals for the stores.
concepts.work: If EOQ is 1,000 and annual demand 25,000, the firm places 25 orders a year.

concepts.title: Selective control and modern techniques
body: ABC analysis classifies items by value: A items (few, high value — tight control), B items (moderate), C items (many, low value — simple control). VED (vital, essential, desirable) and FSN (fast, slow, non-moving) classify by criticality and movement.
Just-in-time (JIT) aims to receive materials only when needed, cutting holding costs but requiring reliable suppliers. Inventory turnover ratio and days of inventory monitor efficiency.
Perpetual inventory and periodic physical verification detect discrepancies; obsolete and slow-moving stock is reviewed for disposal.
concepts.analogy: Control effort should follow value and criticality, not item count.
concepts.work: A pharma maker keeps vital active ingredients under VED "vital" status even if low value.

illustrations.title: EOQ versus a bulk discount
illustrations.q: Annual demand 25,000 units; price ₹100; ordering cost ₹400 per order; carrying cost 20% of price a year. Compute EOQ and total relevant cost. The supplier offers a 2% discount on orders of 2,500 units. Should it be accepted?

solution.text: EOQ = √(2 × 25,000 × 400 ÷ 20) = 1,000 units. Accept the discount: it saves ₹41,500 a year.

jobs.title: Stock review
jobs.situation: A distributor's inventory days have risen from 45 to 75.
steps: Run an ABC and FSN analysis.
Recompute EOQ and re-order levels for A items.
jobs.takeaway: Rising inventory days usually hide a few slow-moving high-value items.

options: Few in number but high in value
mcqs.explain: A items typically form a small share of items but most of the value. In practice: control tightly.

options: Reliable suppliers and short lead times
mcqs.explain: JIT minimises stock, so supply reliability is critical. In practice: works best with nearby vendors.

options: Interest on funds tied in stock
mcqs.explain: Holding stock ties up funds, space and insurance. In practice: often expressed as % of value.
Fast, slow and non-moving items. In practice: non-moving stock is reviewed for disposal.

mcqs.explain: All relevant costs change with order size. In practice: carrying cost per unit may fall with the price.

viva.q: What is the main risk of JIT?
viva.model: Production may stop if suppliers fail to deliver on time, since little buffer stock is held.

cases.title: Sunrise Bakery
cases.case: Sunrise Bakery uses 7,200 kg of flour a year; each order costs ₹250; flour costs ₹40/kg; carrying cost is 25% of price a year. Lead time is 5 days; daily usage averages 20 kg and peaks at 30 kg.

mcqs.explain: Carrying cost ₹10 a kg; √(2 × 7,200 × 250 ÷ 10) = √3,60,000 = 600 kg. In practice: round to bag sizes.
